prompt: How do you turn on Roblox's Server Authority mode, which other settings does it force, and where should gameplay logic that the client predicts live? Say which clock that logic should use.
answer_key: Enable it by setting Workspace.AuthorityMode to Server.

It forces these settings: NextGenerationReplication enabled, PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem enabled, SignalBehavior Deferred, UseFixedSimulation enabled, StreamingEnabled enabled. Naming at least 3 of the 5 earns full credit; 1-2 earns partial.

Core logic goes in functions bound with RunService:BindToSimulation(), in a ModuleScript that runs on both client and server. The client predicts ahead of the server and rolls back and resimulates when it mispredicts.

Use time(), which is synchronised, fixed-step and rewinds during resimulation, not tick()/os.clock()/os.time(). Instance:Destroy(), reparenting and UserInputService events are not allowed inside the bound simulation; use InputActions for input.

Server Authority (full release July 9, 2026) is opt-in: in Workspace properties, Server Authority section, set AuthorityMode = Server. It forces five settings: NextGenerationReplication = Enabled, PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem = Enabled, SignalBehavior = Deferred, StreamingEnabled = Enabled, UseFixedSimulation = Enabled (so you inherit all streaming and deferred-signal bugs).
Predicted gameplay logic goes in a function registered with RunService:BindToSimulation(fn), shared by client and server (e.g. a ModuleScript in ReplicatedStorage required by both). It can be re-run during resimulation, so it must be deterministic: read input from InputAction objects (not UserInputService), keep custom state in attributes on predicted instances (first 64 replicate, names/strings max 50 chars), no Destroy/reparent/EquipTool inside it (record intent, destroy in PostSimulation on server). Clock: use time() (simulation time); not tick(), os.time(), os.clock() or task.wait timing. VFX/sounds go in RenderStepped and must tolerate rollbacks. (Server Authority and Input Migration 2026.)

prompt: Roblox is converting its default player scripts (character controls) to the Input Action System. Which property controls this, what is the rollout timeline, and what existing code is at risk of breaking?
answer_key: The property is Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem. Setting it to Enabled opts in; in phase 1, after the June 2026 IAS full release, it defaults to Disabled.
Timeline: in phase 2 (ETA early 2027) the default becomes Enabled, which is potentially breaking. In phase 3 (ETA mid 2027) the property is removed and every place gets the new scripts.

At risk: code that references the old player scripts or legacy PlayerModule internals (for example require(PlayerModule):GetControls()), and code that relies on old input-sinking behaviour. Forked player scripts need StarterPlayer.CreateDefaultPlayerModule set to Disabled to keep custom controls.

responses.R1:
The switch is the StarterPlayer property that makes the default PlayerModule (ControlModule and camera input) use Input Action System instances (InputContext/InputAction/InputBinding) instead of ContextActionService and UserInputService bindings. It is set to Default/Enabled/Disabled, in the same way other rollout properties work.
Timeline: it started as opt-in (Enabled). Then Default is flipped to mean on for experiences that haven't opted out. Later the old path is removed and the opt-out goes away. Opt out with Disabled for now if you need time, and test with Enabled.
Code at risk:
- Forked or modified PlayerModule / ControlModule copies in StarterPlayerScripts.
- Code that requires PlayerModule internals (GetControls, the activeController, ControlModule:GetMoveVector internals, keyboard/touch module paths).
- ContextActionService:BindActionAtPriority calls that override default move/jump keys, or that rely on sinking the default bindings.
- Code that looks for the default TouchGui/thumbstick/jump button by name.
- UserInputService checks that assume the default scripts don't sink input.

At risk: code that calls require(PlayerModule):GetControls() or otherwise reaches into the ControlModule; code relying on the old input sinking/priority (ContextActionService binds that override movement keys, UserInputService gameProcessed assumptions); and forked or customized PlayerModule copies. Forked player scripts must set StarterPlayer.CreateDefaultPlayerModule appropriately (Disabled) or be migrated.

prompt: What did Roblox's October 2026 TextChatService update change for games that read chat message text or use a custom chat UI, and what is the rollout timeline?
answer_key: You opt in by setting TextChatService.PlatformIntegratedChat to Enabled. Once opted in, code cannot read message content: TextChatMessage.Text (and .Translation) return an empty string (not nil) and a warning appears in Output.
OnIncomingMessage and Player.Chatted are unsupported; use TextChatCommands instead. TextChatMessage.PrefixText is also unsupported, and an official prefix system is planned.
Custom chat UI should move to TextChannelWindow, a native window you can place and size and point at a TextChannel through its Target property.
Timeline: test now. In February 2027 all games are opted in automatically, with an opt-out available. From May 2027 the updated TextChatService is the only way to have custom chat.

responses.R1: With platform-integrated chat on, TextChatMessage.Text and .Translation return an empty string to experience code, so OnIncomingMessage/MessageReceived and Player.Chatted no longer give you message text (no reading text for custom filters, logs, or chat-parsed commands). Use TextChatCommand for admin/commands. Custom chat UIs must move to the TextChannelWindow-based customization rather than rendering message text themselves. Timeline: opt-in testing now through ~Feb 2027, default-on Feb 2027 (some wording says March), required ~May 2027.
responses.R2:
I'm not confident about the details of an October 2026 update. My understanding is that TextChatService became the only chat path: LegacyChatService is fully retired. Message text that clients receive is filtered for each recipient and controlled by safety and age-check rules, so a message can arrive empty or be withheld for some users.
What it means for your game:
- Games that read message text (TextChatMessage.Text in OnIncomingMessage, MessageReceived or commands) must handle text that is filtered, delayed or empty for some recipients, and must not depend on raw unfiltered text.
- Custom chat UIs must render from TextChatService events and keep the required safety elements (filtering, report/mute and the age-based chat restrictions). They must not reconstruct chat from your own remotes.
- The rollout is staged: opt-in or announcement first, then default on, then enforced across all experiences a few weeks later.
Check the DevForum announcement for exact dates.
responses.R3:
October 2026 (DevForum, Oct 21) announced "platform-integrated chat": TextChatService.PlatformIntegratedChat.
When enabled: Roblox renders all chat, in the default window or a TextChannelWindow you place in your own ScreenGui/SurfaceGui (Target = a TextChannel); custom UIs can no longer draw messages. TextChatMessage.Text and .Translation return "" (with a warning), PrefixText is unsupported; OnIncomingMessage and Player.Chatted no longer give text for moderation/admin commands; no API returns message content on client or server. Commands must use TextChatCommand; SendAsync presets/chat wheels move to Quick Words. All user-to-user chat must go through TextChatService; non-chat player text (signs, pet names) must be filtered and rate-limited to one submission per minute or routed through a TextChannel. The property is Studio-only (not scriptable).
Timeline: opt-in testing now until February 2027; February 2027 default on for all games with an opt-out; May 2027 required (the post also mentions opt-out "before March 2027", so March is possible). Native prefixes/role badges planned early Feb 2027, message history end of 2026. Don't build new features that read message text. (Text Chat Customization with TextChatService; Policy and Age Rules 2026)
responses.R4: The October 2026 TextChatService update tightened access to raw message text. Messages are filtered and delivered per recipient, so TextChatMessage.Text is the filtered, recipient-appropriate string. Games must not show or store unfiltered text, and must not build their own message pipeline over RemoteEvents. Custom chat UIs have to render messages that come through TextChatService (MessageReceived/OnIncomingMessage, TextChannel:SendAsync) and respect the age and chat-eligibility checks (CanUserChatAsync / CanUsersChatAsync, TextChannel:CanSendMessage gating). Treat Text as read-only display data, and use Metadata / OnIncomingMessage properties for styling instead of rewriting text. Legacy Chat is fully gone. Rollout: announced with an opt-in period, then enabled by default for all experiences, with the legacy behaviour removed a few months later. Test your custom UI under the new setting before enforcement. I am not certain of the exact dates.
responses.R5: It introduced platform-integrated chat, opted into with TextChatService.PlatformIntegratedChat = Enabled (opt-in in Studio). Under it, TextChatMessage.Text and .Translation return "" with a warning, PrefixText is unsupported, and OnIncomingMessage / Player.Chatted no longer expose message text for your own moderation or parsing. Custom chat UIs must move to the TextChannelWindow model, preset messages become Quick Words, and chat commands should use TextChatCommand. Games that parse chat text or draw their own chat bubbles and windows will break. Timeline: opt-in now until Feb 2027, default on in Feb 2027 with an opt-out (an opt-out until about March 2027 was also mentioned), and mandatory around May 2027. Don't build new features that read TextChatMessage.Text.

Custom chat UIs can no longer draw messages themselves; you must use the Roblox-rendered chat window (TextChannelWindow-style customization) instead. prompt: Since mid-2026, how are DataStore request limits and storage limits calculated for a Roblox experience? Give the write-request budget formula and say how UpdateAsync counts against the budgets.
answer_key: Request budgets are experience-wide: they scale with total CCU across all servers and, since 29 July 2026, are shared with Open Cloud requests. Per-server limits still exist and can be configured, for example with SetRateLimitForRequestType.

Per-minute formula is base + CCU x multiplier: write = 300 + 20 x CCU and read = 300 + 40 x CCU (list = 300 + 2 x CCU, remove = 300 + 40 x CCU). Full credit needs the correct write multiplier and base 300; a base of 250 earns partial credit (see README, disputed items).
Each UpdateAsync call uses one read and one write.
Storage limit = 500 MB + 1 MB x lifetime users, up from a 100 MB baseline. Only the latest version of each key counts toward it.

responses.R1: Limits are now per experience, not per server (per-experience access limits Dec 2025; storage enforced April 2026; July 29, 2026 update unified in-game and Open Cloud requests into one shared per-experience budget and raised the base to 300). Per minute: Read 300 + 40 x CCU; Write 300 + 20 x CCU; List 300 + 2 x CCU; Remove 300 + 40 x CCU. UpdateAsync counts as one read AND one write. Storage: 500 MB + 1 MB per lifetime player. Per key: value up to 4 MB, write throughput 4 MB/min. Open Cloud jobs spend the same budget as live servers, so throttle bulk jobs with GetRequestBudgetForRequestType. (Source: Data and Cloud Changes 2025-2026.)
responses.R2: In mid-2026 the limits moved from per-server to experience-wide budgets that scale with the experience's audience. Storage: a base allowance plus a per-user amount, roughly 100 MB + 1 MB x lifetime unique users. Request limits: experience-wide per-minute budgets for each request type (read, write, list, remove), sized by concurrent users. The write budget per minute is roughly a base amount plus a per-concurrent-user amount, about 60 + 10 x CCU. That is the old per-server formula (60 + numPlayers x 10 per minute) applied experience-wide. UpdateAsync does both a read and a write, so it consumes both the read budget and the write budget. GetRequestBudgetForRequestType still reports what remains. Check the Data Stores limits page for the exact constants.
responses.R3:
Since 2026, DataStore limits are calculated per experience and scale with audience instead of being a flat per-server allowance.
- Storage: base 100 MB plus 1 MB per lifetime unique user (lifetime users x 1 MB + 100 MB).
- Requests: an experience-wide budget per minute that scales with concurrent users. The classic per-server write budget is 60 + numPlayers x 10 requests/min (Set/Increment/Remove/Update), with similar formulas for Get (60 + 10n), GetSorted (5 + 2n) and List (5 + 2n). There are also per-key limits (about 1 write per 6 seconds per key) and a 4 MB value size cap.
- UpdateAsync counts against both the read (Get) and the write (Set) budgets, because it does a read and a conditional write. If the transform returns nil, nothing is written.
Check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before bursts, batch per-player data into one key, and back off when the budget is low.

Write budget = 300 + 20 x CCU per minute (some docs list 250 + 20 x CCU; design for the lower). Read = 300 + 40 x CCU, List = 300 + 2 x CCU, Remove = 300 + 40 x CCU. - Write: 300 + 20 x CCU

- Remove: 300 + 40 x CCU

prompt: My Roblox game sells loot crates for Gems. Gems can be bought with Robux, and there is also a 'Luck Potion' developer product that improves crate odds. What do Roblox's paid random item rules require me to show players, and what must I check for each player?
answer_key: The rules apply because Gems can be bought with Robux. Indirect purchases count too, including in-game currency bought with Robux, keys, re-roll tokens and spin tickets.

Before the player spends, show every possible outcome with its numerical odds as a percentage. The percentages must sum to exactly 100%; rounding is allowed if a disclaimer is shown. Long lists can sit behind a descriptively labelled pop-up, such as a 'Details' button, but not a bare (i) icon.
Luck Potion: explain its numerical effect before purchase, and update the displayed odds dynamically while it is active.

Per player, check PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync(). If ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted is true, block the purchase or use a permitted alternative (free earnable path, fixed disclosed order, sell items directly). If IsPaidItemTradingAllowed is false, don't let that player trade paid outcomes.

Before purchase show every possible outcome with numerical odds as percentages summing to 100% (rounding allowed with a disclaimer); long lists may sit behind a clearly labelled Info/Details button, not a bare (i) icon. The Luck Potion is an odds modifier: explain its effect numerically before purchase, and while it is active the displayed crate odds must update to the boosted values. One-time outcomes must update remaining odds for that player. Per player, check PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync: if ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted is true, block or hide the paid crate/potion (or offer a free earnable path, fixed disclosed order, or direct purchase); if IsPaidItemTradingAllowed is false, block trading of paid outcomes. Enforce server-side; drive roll and displayed odds from one table. (Source: Policy and Age Rules 2026.)
responses.R2: Because Gems are buyable with Robux, Gem-priced crates are paid random items (earnable Gems don't exempt them), and the Luck Potion is covered too. Before purchase, show every possible item with numeric odds totalling 100% (behind a clearly labelled Info/Odds button if long, not a bare icon). For the Luck Potion, show base and boosted odds numerically before buying it, and displayed odds must reflect the active boost. Drive both the roll and the display from one server odds table. Per player, on the server call PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync and block paid crates where ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted is true (treat missing/errors as restricted, fail closed); gate trading of those items on IsPaidItemTradingAllowed == true. Re-check in each purchase/trade handler (not client-only); grant via ProcessReceipt.

prompt: What are Roblox Kids and Roblox Select accounts, and what do a creator and a game need in order to be available to those users?
answer_key: Roblox Kids covers ages 5-8 and Roblox Select covers ages 9-15. Both were announced in April 2026 and rolled out from early June 2026; exact ages vary by region.
Kids accounts can only play games with Minimal or Mild content maturity labels. Select accounts can play games up to and including Moderate.
The creator must be ID-verified, have two-step verification enabled and keep an active Roblox Plus subscription.

The game must pass a three-step selection process, which includes real-time evaluation of how users aged 16+ interact with it. Social hangouts, games about sensitive issues and free-form drawing games are excluded by default.

To reach them (all-ages release, per Creator Hub, Oct 2026):
- Creator: account in good standing and 2+ days old; age check (facial age estimation if under 18, government ID if 18+); 2-Step Verification on; and either two consecutive months of Roblox Plus/Premium or a refundable per-game publishing fee (1,000 Robux per docs/announcement).
- Game: full Maturity & Compliance Questionnaire with rating Minimal or Mild for Kids, Minimal/Mild/Moderate 9+ for Select; pass the Kids and Select evaluation: a trial phase available only to age-checked 16+ users, where it must attract enough highly engaged players (thresholds vary by source, e.g. 250 unique plays / 500 HEPs in 60 days, keep eligibility with 25 over 60 days). Selection excludes social hangouts, sensitive-issue and free-form drawing games by default; communication is off by default for Kids. Creator needs ID verification, 2-step verification and an active Roblox Plus subscription. Game needs a completed, accurate maturity & compliance questionnaire with an appropriate label (Minimal/Mild for Kids, up to Moderate for Select) and must meet the selection criteria.

prompt: How does Roblox's Creator Rewards program pay creators, and what are the current DevEx rates (the standard rate and the 2026 US 18+ rate)?
answer_key: Creator Rewards replaced Engagement-Based Payouts (and Creator Affiliates). The Daily Engagement Reward, which started 24 July 2025, pays 5 Robux per day for each Active Spender who plays at least 10 minutes, where the game is one of the first 3 they launch that day. An Active Spender has made at least USD 9.99 of qualifying purchases in the past 60 days and is not a new or reactivated user.

Audience Expansion Reward: 35% of the first USD 100 of a new or reactivated user's qualifying purchases during their first 60 days. Conditions: the user joins through the creator's Share Link (or a first-session join), plays 10+ minutes, the game averages 100+ DAU and the owner is ID-verified. Rewards are held for 60 days.
Standard DevEx rate: USD 0.0038 per Robux (USD 0.38 per 100).

US 18+ rate: USD 0.0054 per Robux (USD 0.54 per 100), from 8 June 2026. It applies to spend by age-checked 18+ US players on passes, developer products, subscriptions and private servers in games that meet the R15 avatar requirement. Avatar items do not qualify.

responses.R1:
Creator Rewards (launched 2025, replacing Engagement-Based Payouts) pays in Robux, from Roblox, on top of normal sales revenue. It has two parts:
1. Daily engagement rewards: payouts based on the share of time that active spenders (users who spent Robux recently, including Premium members) spend in your experience.
2. Audience expansion rewards: payouts for bringing new users, or lapsed users returning, to Roblox through your experience (for example via shared links).
Payouts are calculated daily and credited after a holding period. Eligible experiences must be public, meet monetization eligibility and follow policy.
DevEx: the standard rate is about $0.0038 per Robux (raised from $0.0035 in 2025), so 100,000 Robux is roughly $380. The 2026 boosted rate for US creators aged 18+ is higher, about $0.0045 per Robux, but I am not certain of that number; check the DevEx page.

Rewards have a ~60-day hold before cashing out. DevEx: standard rate $0.0038 per earned Robux (legacy $0.0035 for older balances); from June 2026 US creators 18+ get $0.0054 per qualifying earned Robux. Minimum 30,000 Robux to cash out.

prompt: When should you use UpdateAsync instead of SetAsync for Roblox player data, and what rules must the UpdateAsync transform function follow?
answer_key: SetAsync overwrites without looking at the current value, so two servers setting the same key at once can make data inconsistent. UpdateAsync reads the current value first, which makes it safer when several servers may write the same key.
The transform function can be called several times (it reruns if another server updated the key in between), so it must have no side effects outside its return value.
The transform function cannot yield: no task.wait() and no other yielding calls inside it.

prompt: I have a turret model (not a player character) whose joints are Motor6Ds driven by an AnimationController with an Animator. answer_key: The Animator overwrites Motor6D.Transform every frame, after RunService.PreAnimation and before PreSimulation. Values written elsewhere in the frame, such as Heartbeat (post-simulation), are replaced before they take effect.

Write procedural offsets in RunService.PreSimulation (formerly Stepped), which runs after the Animator has written Transform and before physics or rendering use it. end)

prompt: A sword-swing animation and the default walk animation both animate the right arm. While walking, the swing looks weak or doesn't show. Explain how Roblox decides which animation wins on a limb, and how weights work.
answer_key: Priority order from lowest to highest: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. Core is the lowest even though its enum value is 1000.
On each limb, the highest-priority playing track wins. Set the swing to Action or higher, in the Animation Editor or through AnimationTrack.Priority.
Tracks with the same priority are blended by weight, set through AnimationTrack:Play(fadeTime, weight) or AdjustWeight (WeightTarget defaults to 1; weight 0 shows nothing).

responses.R1: Roblox blends tracks per joint by priority. For each Motor6D, only tracks with the highest AnimationPriority that animate that joint count (Action4 > Action3 > Action2 > Action > Movement > Idle > Core). Lower-priority tracks are overridden on that joint. If the sword swing and walk share a priority (for example both Movement or Core, or the swing was left at Core), they blend by weight, so the swing gets averaged with the walk and looks weak. Within the same priority, each track's effective weight (set with AdjustWeight or Play(fadeTime, weight)) determines its share. Weights are normalized among tracks of the same priority, and fading ramps weight in and out. Fix: set the swing to Action or higher, either in the Animation Editor or with track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action before Play, and play it at weight 1. Also make sure the walk animation isn't at a higher priority, and that the swing actually keys the right-arm joints (only keyed joints override).
responses.R2:
Each AnimationTrack has a Priority (Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4). For each joint, only tracks with the highest priority among those that animate that joint are used. Lower-priority tracks are ignored on that joint. If equal-priority tracks animate the same joint, they are blended by weight.
The default walk is Movement. If your swing was exported as Core, Idle or Movement, the walk either overrides it or blends with it, so it looks weak or invisible. Fix: set the swing to Action (or higher), in the Animation Editor before export or with track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action after loading.
Weights: track:Play(fadeTime, weight, speed) or track:AdjustWeight(w, fade). Within one priority level, joint poses are blended in proportion to the tracks' effective weights (WeightCurrent, which ramps during fade-in/out). A track with weight 1 alone fully poses the joint; two equal tracks at weight 1 each contribute 50%. Weight does not let a lower priority beat a higher one. Keyframes that don't key a joint leave that joint free for lower priorities.
responses.R3: Roblox resolves per joint by AnimationPriority (Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4). The highest-priority playing tracks that animate a joint claim weight first; only leftover weight (1 - their total) passes to lower priorities. The default walk is Movement priority; if your swing was authored/loaded as Core or Idle (or Movement and blending equally), walk wins or splits the arm, so the swing looks weak. Fix: set the swing track's Priority to Action (or higher), play it at weight 1 (AdjustWeight/Play(fade, weight)). Weight: within the same priority tracks blend proportionally by weight; a higher-priority track at weight 0.6 gives a 60/40 mix with the lower layer; at 1 it fully overrides that joint. Only joints with keyframes in the track are affected, so the legs still walk.
responses.R4: The Animator blends per joint. For each joint, only tracks that actually key that joint compete. The highest AnimationPriority among those tracks wins: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. A higher-priority track at weight 1 fully owns the joint. If its effective weight is below 1, the remainder goes to lower-priority tracks, so Action at 0.6 lets walk show 0.4. Tracks of equal priority blend by their relative weights: they're summed and normalised, and a total below 1 pulls toward the rest pose. Effective weight is the weight set by Play(fadeTime, weight) or AdjustWeight, multiplied by the fade-in progress. The swing looks weak because it's probably the same priority as walk (Movement or Core, often the default when authored), so the two average out. Or its weight or fade is low. Fix: set the swing track's Priority to Action (or higher) before or when playing, play it at weight 1 with a short fade, and key only the upper-body joints so the legs still walk.
responses.R5: Each joint is driven by the playing tracks with the highest AnimationPriority that actually key that joint: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. A higher-priority track overrides lower ones only on limbs it has keyframes for. Tracks at the same priority blend in proportion to their weights; lower priorities only get whatever weight is left if the higher-priority tracks' total weight is below 1. Weight is set by track:Play(fadeTime, weight) or track:AdjustWeight(weight, fadeTime); fades ramp it. prompt: My Blender model imports into Roblox Studio as an FBX about 100 times too big. Why, and what export settings does Roblox recommend?
answer_key: With default settings, Blender's FBX export often imports into Studio at an unexpectedly large scale (a unit-scale mismatch).
Recommended fix: in the FBX exporter, set Transform > Apply Scalings to 'FBX Unit Scale' and leave every other scale value at 1.0.

Alternatives: an export Transform Scale of 0.01, or a scene Unit Scale of 0.01. Caveats: re-imports into other tools may need scaling back up, working at 0.01 can cause Blender camera issues, and methods should not be stacked.
glTF/GLB export does not need these extra scaling settings.

responses.R1: Blender's default unit scale is meters (1 unit = 1 m), and FBX stores centimeters. Roblox's importer interprets FBX units differently from Blender's scale factor, so you get a factor of 100 (1 m becomes 100 'cm' studs). Fix on export, using Roblox's recommended Blender FBX settings: Scene Unit Scale 0.01 with Unit System Metric (or apply scale), and in the FBX exporter set Apply Scalings to 'FBX Units Scale' and Scale = 1 (or 0.01 depending on your scene units). Also set Forward -Z and Up Y, enable Apply Unit and Apply Transform, select Mesh and Armature only, turn off Add Leaf Bones, and apply scale (Ctrl+A) beforehand. Alternatively, in the Studio 3D Importer, set the import scale or World/File units (the importer has a scale option). Now that the importer supports it, glTF/GLB is preferred and doesn't have this cm/m mismatch.
responses.R2: Unit mismatch: Blender works in metres and the FBX exporter writes a unit-scale factor (centimetre-based), so the importer ends up multiplying by ~100. Recommended: set up the scene so 1 Blender unit = 1 stud (Unit Scale 1); apply rotation & scale (Ctrl+A) and put the root at the origin; FBX export with Apply Scalings = 'FBX Units Scale', Forward -Z / Up Y, Apply Unit; for rigs Add Leaf Bones off, Key All Bones on, Simplify 0. In the Studio 3D Importer check the Scale Unit (Studs). Or export glTF/GLB instead. Don't rescale rigs afterwards in Studio.
responses.R3:
Unit mismatch. Blender's default scene is 1 unit = 1 metre with Unit Scale 1.0, and FBX stores centimetres, so the exporter writes your model with a 100x scale factor; Studio reads the FBX units and 1 Blender metre ends up ~100 studs (often combined with unapplied object scale).
Roblox-recommended Blender setup: Scene Properties > Units: Unit Scale 0.01 (so 1 Blender unit maps to 1 stud), set before modelling/rigging; apply transforms (Ctrl+A > All Transforms). FBX export: Limit to Selected Objects, Apply Scalings = FBX Units Scale (or FBX All), Forward -Z, Up Y, Apply Unit on, Apply Transform on, object types Mesh/Armature; rigs: Add Leaf Bones off; Path Mode Copy + Embed Textures for textures.
Check the size in the 3D Importer preview (you can also adjust scale/file units there), or export .glb, which uses metres and imports at sensible size. Don't just shrink rigs in Studio, since animation data stays at the wrong scale.
responses.R4:
Blender works in meters with Unit Scale 1. The FBX exporter writes in centimeters by default (a FBX unit scale of 100), and Studio reads 1 unit as 1 stud. A 2 m model can therefore come in as 200 studs.
Fixes recommended in the Roblox docs:
- Scene Properties: Unit System Metric, with Unit Scale 0.01 (and Length in centimeters), so Blender units match the FBX cm the way Roblox expects. Or keep Unit Scale 1 and set the exporter's Scale to 0.01.
- In the FBX export: Apply Scalings = FBX Units Scale (or "FBX All"), Forward = -Z Forward, Up = Y Up, Apply Unit checked, and Apply Transform as needed.
- Before exporting, apply rotation and scale (Ctrl+A > All Transforms) so objects export at scale 1.
- For rigs, apply scale on the armature too, and keep the armature's scale at 1.
- In the Studio importer, check the scale or "Use Importer Units" setting in the 3D Importer's options as a last-resort correction.
Note that 1 stud is about 0.28 m, so model to Roblox's proportions (a character is about 5 studs tall).
responses.R5: Unit mismatch in the chain: Blender scene units (metres) vs the FBX exporter's unit scale (FBX stores centimetres; default 'All Local' scaling adds a x100 factor) vs the Studio importer's assumptions. Mixing scale methods gives 100x. Fix at the source, not with Model:ScaleTo in Studio (never rescale animated rigs: clip translations stay in old units). Recommended: 1 Blender unit = 1 stud (unit system None, or Metric with 1 m = 1 stud) and never change mid-project; FBX Apply Scalings: FBX Unit Scale; transforms applied (scale 1, rotation 0); model front facing -Y; Add Leaf Bones off; for animation Simplify 0; Studio 3D Importer Scale Unit = Studs (and check its preview size). Or export GLB, which avoids most FBX scale issues. Verify against a ~5-stud R15 avatar after import. (AI Pitfalls - Assets and Import; Exporting FBX vs GLB.)

Blender's default scene is metric (1 unit = 1 m) and the FBX exporter writes centimeter-based unit scale (FBX unit = cm, scale 100 with "All Local"/default), while Studio's importer treats units as studs, so the unit chain (scene units, FBX unit scale, importer Scale Unit) multiplies by ~100.

prompt: I exported a .glb from Blender. In Roblox Studio my Mirror and Bevel modifiers are missing: only half the mesh is there and the edges are sharp. Why, and what is the catch with fixing it in the exporter?
answer_key: Blender's glTF exporter option 'Apply Modifiers' (export_apply) is off by default, so the base mesh is exported without the modifiers evaluated.
Enable Apply Modifiers (under Data > Mesh) to export the evaluated mesh. It applies all modifiers except Armature, so skinning still exports.

Catch: enabling Apply Modifiers prevents shape keys (morph targets) from being exported. Meshes that need shape keys must have those modifiers handled another way, for example applied manually beforehand.

responses.R1: Modifiers are non-destructive and live only in Blender. A .glb contains the mesh data only. If the exporter doesn't apply modifiers, Roblox gets the base mesh: half the model before Mirror, and unbeveled sharp edges. Fix: tick Apply Modifiers in the glTF exporter (Include/Data > Mesh > Apply Modifiers), or apply them manually (Ctrl+A > Apply) on a copy before exporting. prompt: Write a short server-side Luau handler for a RemoteEvent named BuyItem. The client fires it with (itemId, quantity) to buy an item with in-game coins. Make it exploit-resistant.
answer_key: Uses OnServerEvent's automatic first `player` parameter, and takes the price from a server-side catalogue. A price or player sent by the client is never trusted.
Validates type and structure: itemId must exist in the server catalogue; quantity must be a number that is finite (math.isfinite or a NaN check), an integer and within sane bounds (> 0, capped).

Checks context against server-held state before acting: enough coins for the total cost (plus any other conditions, such as distance to the shop). Coins are deducted and the item granted on the server.
Rate-limits each player on the server (cooldown or token bucket). Client-side limits alone are not enough.

-- ServerScriptService
local RS = game:GetService('ReplicatedStorage')
local Items = require(game.ServerStorage.ItemCatalog) -- [id] = {price=..}
local BuyItem = RS.Remotes.BuyItem
local last = {}

BuyItem.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, itemId, quantity)
  local now = os.clock()
  if last[player] and now - last[player] < 0.25 then return end
  last[player] = now
  if typeof(itemId) ~= 'string' or typeof(quantity) ~= 'number' then return end
  if quantity ~= quantity or quantity % 1 ~= 0 or quantity < 1 or quantity > 99 then return end
  local item = Items[itemId]
  if not item then return end
  local coins = player:FindFirstChild('leaderstats') and player.leaderstats:FindFirstChild('Coins')
  if not coins then return end
  local cost = item.price * quantity
  if coins.Value < cost then return end
  coins.Value -= cost
  Inventory.add(player, itemId, quantity) -- server-owned data
end)

game:GetService('Players').PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(p) last[p] = nil end)

prompt: Debug this. I set MeshPart.RenderFidelity = Precise on my hero meshes, but in my published game they still drop to lower detail at a distance, and changing the property seems to do nothing. What is going on?
answer_key: Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs (mesh streaming with improved cloud LoDs, opt-in since April 2026) is Enabled. In that mode RenderFidelity is ignored on every MeshPart and meshes go through the new transcoder instead.

RenderFidelity is planned for removal in a later phase (Default is planned to map to Enabled). To compare, toggle the Workspace property (Studio asks for a restart), test in Studio, and report broken meshes with asset IDs.

responses.R1: RenderFidelity isn't a normal runtime property: it can only be set in Studio/by plugins before publishing (scripts can't change it at runtime, and setting it in Studio may require re-upload/geometry processing), so script changes do nothing. More importantly, Precise only requests full detail; the client still lowers detail based on the player's graphics quality level, memory pressure and Roblox's streaming/LOD systems (model streaming LOD, mesh LOD on low-end devices), so on lower settings or mobile meshes still drop detail at distance. Studio typically runs at high quality so you don't see it there. Check: the property is actually set on the published MeshParts (not on a different copy), test with low graphics quality, and use ModelStreamingMode = Persistent / Atomic for key models; reduce mesh triangle counts so the low LOD looks acceptable. Note: in my lookup the vault had no note explaining this exact symptom; this is general knowledge.
responses.R2: RenderFidelity is not scriptable at runtime: it is only honoured when set in Studio before publishing, so script writes (or changing it in a running game) do nothing. Precise only disables that mesh's own fidelity reduction; other systems still drop detail at distance in live clients: the device's graphics quality level and memory-pressure LOD on weaker devices, and with StreamingEnabled the Model.LevelOfDetail (StreamingMesh/Automatic) swaps distant models for low-detail impostor meshes. Fix: set Precise in Studio and republish, set the hero Model's LevelOfDetail = Disabled (ModelStreamingMode Atomic/Persistent if needed), and test at realistic graphics quality. Use Precise sparingly (performance cost).
responses.R3:
RenderFidelity is being superseded by mesh streaming and improved cloud LoDs (announced April 27, 2026). Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs (Default/Enabled/Disabled): when Enabled, every mesh in the published game uses the cloud LoD transcoder and mesh streaming, and MeshPart.RenderFidelity is ignored, so Precise does nothing and meshes drop to lower LoDs at distance. Phase 2 (planned around July 2026) maps Default to Enabled, and Phase 3 removes the property and RenderFidelity. Studio may also look different from live (streaming applies in published experiences; reported bugs of meshes stuck at lowest LoD).
What to do: check the effective value of Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs; if you need it, set Disabled while the opt-out exists (temporary), but plan for removal: budget triangles at the source, design the meshes so cloud LoDs look acceptable (clean silhouettes, no thin details that collapse), and delete code that sets/branches on RenderFidelity (guard any reads with pcall). Collision geometry is unaffected. (Engine and API Changes 2025-2026)
responses.R4: RenderFidelity is not a runtime-scriptable property. It's baked when the MeshPart is created or imported (set it in Studio, via plugins, or in CreateMeshPartAsync options), so setting it from a game script has no effect. Also check that you actually saved and published the Studio edit. Precise does keep the mesh at full detail at any distance. Other things lower detail in a live game: (1) Model streaming LOD. With StreamingEnabled and the parent Model's LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh (or Automatic), distant or unstreamed models are drawn as low-poly imposter meshes regardless of RenderFidelity. Set Model.LevelOfDetail = Disabled (and/or ModelStreamingMode = Persistent) for hero models. (2) Client graphics quality. Low quality levels and mobile devices reduce draw distance and detail, which Studio (often at max quality) doesn't show. (3) Automatic fidelity on other parts, such as unions, accessories and textures (Automatic steps down at about 250 and 500 studs). Verify with a test place on the target device.

Since April 2026 Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs (Default/Enabled/Disabled) exists; when Enabled, every mesh uses the cloud LoD transcoder and mesh streaming and MeshPart.RenderFidelity is ignored, so meshes drop detail with distance/memory regardless of Precise. The real fix is budgeting triangles at the source (clean topology, silhouette-preserving geometry) and not relying on RenderFidelity. Also: RenderFidelity can't be changed by scripts at runtime (set it in Studio before publishing), Studio can show a different LoD than live, and there are reported bugs of meshes stuck at lowest LoD (report with repro). Collision geometry is unaffected. (Engine and API Changes 2025-2026.)

Changing it from a script errors or is ignored, and the engine's distance LOD streaming can still choose lower-detail versions. Also, Precise is a hint: the client may still lower detail under memory pressure or on low graphics quality, and with StreamingEnabled, models can use Model.LevelOfDetail (StreamingMesh) imposters at distance. Several things are going on:
1. RenderFidelity can't be set by scripts at runtime. It's a Studio/plugin-level property that is baked when the mesh part is created or imported. Script assignments in a live game are ignored or error, so "changing it does nothing".
2. More importantly, Roblox's renderer now uses its own automatic mesh LOD and streaming. RenderFidelity is largely legacy: Precise is no longer a guarantee that full detail is kept at distance. 3. With StreamingEnabled, distant models can also be shown as low-detail model LOD imposters (Model.LevelOfDetail = Automatic/StreamingMesh) until they stream in.
What to do:
- Set the property in Studio, not in scripts, and accept that distant LOD is engine-controlled.
- For important hero models, set Model.LevelOfDetail = Disabled and ModelStreamingMode = Persistent (or Atomic) if they shouldn't be imposters.
